_comment: SYNTHETIC — hand-built from Yahoo's documented OAuth error format. NOT a live
capture: Yahoo API access is gated behind an approval application and NO live
call has ever been made from this repo, so no real 401 has ever been seen
here. Replace with a real captured body once access is approved and a token
actually expires. The wording is representative, not verbatim.
AUTHORED 2026-08-11 (not captured on any date).
MODELS: the JSON body returned with HTTP 401 by any /fantasy/v2/ request
made with an expired or revoked access token.
REDACTION: no token, refresh token, client id, client secret or account
identifier appears here — and none may ever be added. This file will sit in
a public git history forever.
WHY THIS IS COMMITTED: an expired access token is NORMAL, not exceptional.
Yahoo access tokens last 3600 seconds and a fifteen-season backfill runs for
far longer than an hour, so a mid-run 401 is an EXPECTED event that must be
handled by refreshing and resuming — never by aborting, and above all never
by recording the resources it interrupted as empty. The client refreshes
proactively with a margin so this ideally never fires; this fixture exists
for when it does anyway (clock skew, a token revoked out from under us, a
server-side session reset).
SHAPE NOTES:
1. This is a JSON object with an 'error' key and NO 'fantasy_content'
envelope. unwrap_content() must RAISE on it rather than return {} — an
error body is not an empty result. ⚠️ Because '_comment' is a real key
in this file, that exception's message will list both '_comment' and
'error' as the top-level keys it found. That is expected; strip the
comment first if the assertion is on the exact message.
2. The machine-readable failure reason is buried in a PROSE description
string — oauth_problem="token_expired" — not in a dedicated code field.
Yahoo's OAuth 2.0 errors still carry OAuth 1.0-era vocabulary. Matching
on substrings is unavoidable here; matching on it is also the reason
redact_text() must be applied before any error body is logged.
THE OTHER BODY THAT MATTERS — the refresh endpoint's failure, which has a
DIFFERENT shape and comes from a different host (api.login.yahoo.com, not
fantasysports.yahooapis.com). It cannot be a second top-level object in this
file, so it is recorded here verbatim for any test that needs it:
{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"Invalid or expired refresh token"}
invalid_grant on refresh means the REFRESH token is dead, which is a
different situation from an expired access token: nothing can be retried,
and a human has to re-consent. oauth.py detects it by substring on the raw
body and raises AuthError with that remedy in the message.
⚠️ Yahoo's own documentation contradicts itself about when this happens —
the OAuth guide says a refresh token persists across a password change,
the FAQ says all refresh tokens are revoked on password change. Assume the
FAQ is right and treat invalid_grant as a normal, expected outcome that
needs re-consent, not as a bug to be retried.
A THIRD FAILURE THIS FILE IS NOT: HTTP 403. That is not an auth problem and
must not be retried as one — it means the authenticated account genuinely
cannot read that resource. Private leagues are readable only by members, so
a season the account never played is permanently unreachable and is recorded
as access_denied, not as a gap to fill in later.

error.description: Please provide valid credentials. OAuth oauth_problem="token_expired", realm="yahooapis.com"
